answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: Pausanias gives this account (from theoi.com), that suggests that Orthia demanded blood sacrifice of humans, which the legendary lawgiver, Lycurgus, switched to scourging youths on the altar:  [3.16.9] I will give other evidence that the Orthia in Lacedaemon is the wooden image from the foreigners. Firstly, Astrabacus and Alopecus, sons of Irbus, son of Amphisthenes, son of Amphicles, son of Agis, when they found the image straightway became insane. Secondly, the Spartan Limnatians, the Cynosurians, and the people of Mesoa and Pitane, while sacrificing to Artemis, fell to quarreling, which led also to bloodshed; many were killed at the altar and the rest died of disease.  [3.16.10] Whereat an oracle was delivered to them, that they should stain the altar with human blood. He used to be sacrificed upon whomsoever the lot fell, but Lycurgus changed the custom to a scourging of the lads, and so in this way the altar is stained with human blood. By them stands the priestess, holding the wooden image. Now it is small and light,  [3.16.11] but if ever the scourgers spare the lash because of a lad's beauty or high rank, then at once the priestess finds the image grow so heavy that she can hardly carry it. She lays the blame on the scourgers, and says that it is their fault that she is being weighed down. So the image ever since the sacrifices in the Tauric land keeps its fondness for human blood. They call it not only Orthia, but also Lygodesma (Willow-bound), because it was found in a thicket of willows, and the encircling willow made the image stand upright.

Yes [specify]: infants and children encompass a large group of sacrifices (n = 30) to this deity but adults (n = 11; men and women) were also recovered from the temple's offerings (Guilliem Arroyo 1999:172)..
Yes [specify]: Human sacrifices were systematically performed at the site.
Yes [specify]: Not allowed - altough never specified, no one could die inside the temenos
Yes [specify]: As a part of the Mesoamerican religious tradition.

questions.name: Other formal burial type:
questions.parent_question: Are formal burials present:

answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: Cave and rock shelter burials with evidence for a variety of treatments including some burial furniture like stone pillows. There is also evidence for large (community-wide) rituals in the form of pits containing ceramics. The pits are, apparently, remarkably consistent in content and form between sites.
Yes [specify]: One example of an ossuary in a cave is in the encyclopedia entry.
Yes [specify]: Domestic cists (less formal than tombs) also are found in domestic contests.

Yes [specify]: Extended family cemeteries have become common since the 1970s. These are often located close to dwellings inhabited by living members of the extended family. At first the grave is densely covered with wreaths and bouquets of artificial flowers. Some time later the grave is concreted over--another ceremony that substitutes for secondary stages of burial no longer practiced. Often the concrete in sculpted into the shape of a totemic being associated with the person's clan.

To other humans there are also actions of gratitude such as clasping the knees

Yes [specify]: “The most frequent vows are those which are made directly with God Himself. These are called magjanji' ni Tuhan and take the form of a promise that, in return for a special favour, the individual will dedicate himself to an act of piety or devotion, as a sign of thanksgiving ( magsukul ). Many kinds of favours may be sought in this way. For example, God may be asked to deliver someone from danger, or to bring him home safely from a difficult journey. If a fishing party fails to return to the village when expected, or is caught in a storm at sea, those at home may make a vow promising a rite of thanksgiving in repayment for its safe return.” (1997) The Bajau Laut: adaptation, history, and fate in a maritime fishing society of south-east Sabah Section: Ritual Vows ( Janji' ) By: Sather, Clifford Page: 288 Published: 1997 Series: South-East Asian social science monographs

Yes [specify]: “Ceremonies in the hills on the part of the chuchqajau , to give thanks to the world during the night and to San Martín in the church. In the house one gives thanks for the harvest. 27 27 Although I was not taken to these ceremonies I heard distant rockets at intervals throughout the night. Specify: 1. Performing the magmaulud rite “Their fulfilment takes the form of a rite of thanksgiving (magmaulud'), described at greater length in Chapter 10, in which male guests are invited to the vow-taker's house to read from the scriptures. Magmaulud is carried out by the house group as a whole under the sponsorship of its nakura'. Failure by the group to fulfil its terms of the vow is regarded as a serious ritual offence, which places the entire group in a state of jeopardy (kabusungan). In this particular case, a chain of events began when two house leaders sought to sponsor a joint rite of thanksgiving but could not agree in which of their two houses the ritual should be held.” (1997) The Bajau Laut: adaptation, history, and fate in a maritime fishing society of south-east Sabah Section: Leadership and the House Group as an Economic and Ritual Unit By: Sather, Clifford Page: 184 Published: 1997 Series: South-East Asian social science monographs 2. Performing the magtimbang rite (similar to magmaulud) “The rite is performed chiefly in connection with childbirth and illness among new-born infants and small children. Like magmaulud , it is essentially a rite of thanksgiving, although it is sometimes also held in anticipation of a favour which has not yet been received.” (1997) The Bajau Laut: adaptation, history, and fate in a maritime fishing society of south-east Sabah Section: Fate and God's Favour By: Sather, Clifford Page: 290 Published: 1997 Series: South-East Asian social science monographs 3. Conducting ceremonies where the cured sick person is bathed in water “If the ceremony is one of thanksgiving for the recovery of a sick person, the ceremony is concluded by the djin bathing the recovered person in seawater followed by a rinse in fresh water. A brief prayer usually accompanies the bathing, which is believed to cleanse the person of the former illness.” (2000) Magosaha: an ethnology of the Tawi-Tawi Sama Dilaut Section: Curing Ceremonies By: Nimmo, Harry Page: 154 Published: 2000 4. Paying tribute to the Lord of the sea by dropping plates, bowls, and saucers into the sea for more fish “For every big catch made in their pag-ambit it is customary among the Badjaos to pay a tribute to their Omboh , or Lord, who they believe has given them the good luck. Usually, a dua-salamat , or thanksgiving, is performed in the house of their headmen. The tribute to the Lord of the sea, Omboh Dilaut , consists of dropping a plate, a bowl, and a saucer in that part of the sea where the group of fish have appeared so that the Omboh will not be angry with them but will give them more fish.” (1989) The lifestyle of the Badjaos: a study of education and culture Section: Economic Life By: Teo, Saladin S. questions.name: Are there any indications that the expression was particularly costly (in terms of time, resources, physical pain involved, or other sacrifice/loss?
questions.parent_question: Are there any behaviors or rituals that people use to express gratitude to god/s or other supernatural agents? (e.g. material tribute/sacrifices, non-material expressions of gratitude, promises/acts of prosociality, etc.)

answer_examples.answer: Specify: Frequent promises of sacrifices, temples, and offerings at temples - often of great value

Specify: 1) Material and monetary cost which involved large quantities of valuable goods- such as gold, jewelry, costly bronze statuettes, precious metal objects, and ritual equipment—were dedicated to temples or as votives to the gods. For example, in the aftermath of military campaigns, the spoils included precious metals weighing hundreds of kilograms, deposited as acts of thanksgiving or atonement. These were not symbolic gestures but involved real and substantial resources for individuals or the community.; 2) Animal and Human Sacrifice: Offering unblemished animals (cattle, sheep, goats, birds) was required and strictly regulated, which meant the loss of prime livestock—assets that represented real economic hardship for many households. In rare but attested cases, human sacrifices were performed, especially in times of crisis, such as the Moabite king sacrificing his son during a siege. These acts represented the ultimate cost, both emotionally and in terms of social/familial loss.; 3) Personal Sacrifice—Time and Labor: Promises to build or repair temples, supply priests, or participate in extensive religious feasts and festivals required significant expenditure of time and collective labor. Such works had community, economic, and political consequences, as resources and manpower were redirected from daily sustenance activities to fulfill religious gratitude.; 4) Pain and Physical Hardship: Beyond the emotional toll of offering prized possessions or loved ones, certain rituals might include bodily suffering. For example, ritual fasting or ascetic practices, as well as evidence of bodily mutilation or self-affliction, are recorded in association with some ancient religious rites.; and 5) Obligatory Reciprocation and Social Risk: The system of gift-giving and reciprocity could be so demanding that it might impoverish or strain individuals who sought to meet the expected standard. Failing to reciprocate at the appropriate level risked shame, loss of status, or even social subservience; thus, the economic and social stakes for participants could be extremely high.
Specify: thanksgiving offerings, 3,000 prostrations, temple donations, or fulfilling vows with time and resources
Specify: Yes, costly in terms of resources and time
Specify: Some early Christians practiced fasting or vigils; some persecuted early Christians saw martyrdom on behalf of their religion as a form of thanksgiving and offering
Specify: Yes, sometimes its costly in terms of resources

Specify: By all means rituals are costly, both monetarily and physically, since they involve alcohol consumption. These costs are greater for cargo holders, but even less committed individuals (e.g., non-specialists) will also experience them

Yes [specify]: Pausanias gives this account (from theoi.com), that suggests that Orthia demanded blood sacrifice of humans, which the legendary lawgiver, Lycurgus, switched to scourging youths on the altar:  [3.16.9] I will give other evidence that the Orthia in Lacedaemon is the wooden image from the foreigners. Firstly, Astrabacus and Alopecus, sons of Irbus, son of Amphisthenes, son of Amphicles, son of Agis, when they found the image straightway became insane. Secondly, the Spartan Limnatians, the Cynosurians, and the people of Mesoa and Pitane, while sacrificing to Artemis, fell to quarreling, which led also to bloodshed; many were killed at the altar and the rest died of disease.  [3.16.10] Whereat an oracle was delivered to them, that they should stain the altar with human blood. He used to be sacrificed upon whomsoever the lot fell, but Lycurgus changed the custom to a scourging of the lads, and so in this way the altar is stained with human blood. By them stands the priestess, holding the wooden image. Now it is small and light,  [3.16.11] but if ever the scourgers spare the lash because of a lad's beauty or high rank, then at once the priestess finds the image grow so heavy that she can hardly carry it. She lays the blame on the scourgers, and says that it is their fault that she is being weighed down. So the image ever since the sacrifices in the Tauric land keeps its fondness for human blood. They call it not only Orthia, but also Lygodesma (Willow-bound), because it was found in a thicket of willows, and the encircling willow made the image stand upright.

questions.name: Other survival condition:
questions.parent_question: Will anyone survive the eschaton:

answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: Only a small group of person with or without Buddhist or Esoteric belief will survive the Buddhist End of Dharma era and start new cycles of human civilization with better and better morality before Maitreya descends to the human realm to attain Buddhahood.
Yes [specify]: For John Wesley it is God's perogative to determine who has been justified by faith.
Yes [specify]: Many Rastafari state that it is only the truly righteous that will survive the judgement event

Yes [specify]: In contemporary Catholic theology and tradition there is no particular focus on the eschaton. Definitions of who will survive or what will exactly take place are not very salient in the discourse or influential in people's beliefs. In general it is clear that the events at the end of the world (many of them violent and tragic) will lead to the death of many people. However, this is not of great importance for the larger narrative because, what matters is that after the Final Judgement, those people who are deemed deserving due to their behaviour in life (regardless of when they lived or died), will be resurrected in body and soul and will live eternally in a new reality or 'Kingdom of God'. Therefore the emphasis is less on survival during the eschaton and more on the eternal life that will be granted after the final judgement to all those who deserve it.

Yes [specify]: All beings continue to reincarnate until they achieve enlightenment, so while individuals in their current manifestation will not survive per se, they will continue to be reborn until all sentient beings achieve awakening.

answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: different spirit types that are a mix of indigenous Tibetan and Indian Buddhist classification schemes.
Yes [specify]: While God and Mary are at the top of the hierarchy, and angels are ranked, the saints are generally domain-specific without hierarchy

Yes [specify]: The beings in the pantheon co-exist rather than being 'organised', except in a spatial sense. Each is associated with particular places where they carried out transformational acts--creating features of the landscape, transforming (parts of) themselves into the landscape, or leaving their power (maarr) in particular places. They rarely interact directly, although sometimes are said to observe each others' activities. The beings of opposite moieties never interact, nor do they enter country belonging to the opposite moiety with very rare exceptions (and cataclysmic consequences). Some are grouped in pairs or sets, for example the Djan'kawu Sisters and the Waagilak Sisters, or Dhamilingu (Frill-neck lizard) and Baaru (saltwater crocodile) who are husband and wife in a particular myth sequence about the spread of fire.

Yes [specify]: Supreme anthropmorphic deity, who also has non-anthropomorphic features simultaneously; less powerful manifestations of supreme deity exist relative to capacities exhibited; semi-divine beings exist that are included in the pantheon
Yes [specify]: It is difficult to fix the Hindu pantheon of Gods in the fix hierarchy or relation.

Yes [specify]: Spatial, visual, conceptual. The Greek pantheon was portrayed and thought of often as a group of gods sitting on high (in the sky, or 'heaven'), and the gods also had their special spheres of activity in the world.

questions.name: Are gestures of interpersonal gratitude explicitly described as a way of repaying/reciprocating/balancing out debts to that person (for what they have given you)?

answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: Thus a person may eat first in one hut and then in another, but eventually he also must show that he is a generous host. No one expresses thanks for what he has eaten, even if choice tidbits have been offered him (430) 430. Bridges (k):240 was acquainted with this custom which is strange to Europeans: “The natives…never express thanks, but on every occasion are prompt to repay [the] services” (1937) The Yahgan: the life and thought of the water nomads of Cape Horn Section: 1. Special Forms of Social Intercourse By: Gusinde, Martin, 1886-1969 Page: 918
Yes [specify]: Though there was no 'payment cleared' in this sense, even as it was understood to form an obligation

Yes [specify]: “The buddi ni intom or gratitude is a value which may not be immediately repayable and reciprocated. But once the debt of gratitude has been ingrained in his heart, one feels that he is totally indebted to the individual in spite of the fact that he may have reciprocated the favor already.” (1989) The lifestyle of the Badjaos: a study of education and culture Section: Values By: Teo, Saladin S. Page: 134 Published: 1989

Yes [specify]: “There is little willingness to provide favors, even to a spouse or close kinsman, without explicit compensation... The periodic weeding of a man’s yard, for example, which a wife considers a standard conjugal duty, is often solicited by the husband and rewarded with both public praise and material “thanks” — e.g., a pot, a carved comb, or a piece of cloth. Goods proffered as “thanks” (tangí) form a special class in Saramaka, somewhere between a free gift and a payment. A special ceremony of “giving thanks” (dá tangí) follows almost every transaction involving goods or services.”  Price, Richard. 1975. “Saramaka Social Structure: Analysis of a Maroon Society in Surinam.” In Caribbean Monograph Series, p. 32

Yes [specify]: Kotta amavasya , literally ‘the New Moon’, the day after ugādi , is an important date in the reckoning of debts and contracts. It is common for people to say “I'll settle my debt with you by kotta amavasya ”. (Telugu Rivalry and tribute: society and ritual in a Telegu village in South India; Section: Minor annual festivals, agricultural ritalsm and private…; Tapper, Bruce Elliot; page: 223).

Yes [specify]: “The professional in any field has definite obligations towards his public. If called upon, he may not refuse his services for any cause except inauspicious omens. He may not demand any fee for his servvices, but must accept whatever compensation is offered. The scale of fees for the more usual services, such as consulting the oracle, performing a simple ceremony “of thanks,” etc., is clearly understood by both practitioner and client; if the client does not know the proper fee for any service that has been performed, he asks. In important cases involving the performance of many ceremonies the fee is agreed upon in advance, as well as the contingent expenses, just as surgeon's fees are agreed upon in our own civilization.” Chichicastenango: a Guatemalan village; Section: Professions; By: Bunzel, Ruth Leah, Page: 78

answer_examples.answer: Specify: Wife / Generosity  “At the other place they’d made fun of him, taunted him. But the Dómbis gave him a wife. Well, they had been so generous with him that he said, “Brother-in-law, catch a chicken and bring it to me.” He did. “Now break its leg and put it under that basket there. Then go bring... [leaves and other secret ingredients].” He also went and gathered ingredients himself. Then he prepared it all until he was satisfied. He said, “Brother-in-law, watch carefully.” And he applied the medicine to the chicken. Every day for seven days. Then they lifted the basket. The chicken ran off tjá tjá tjá tjá ! It didn’t run tíngo tíngo tíngo ! Then he said, “To express my thanks for your generosity, this óbia [medicine] is now yours.””  Price, Richard. 1983. “First-Time: The Historical Vision of an Afro-American People.” In Johns Hopkins Studies in Atlantic History and Culture, p. 126  (Congratulations  This defense by false modesty is matched by special supernatural protection whenever renown (nê) is sought. Even a common woodcarving is marked with a kósi (usually a simple X) which acts to “thank” anyone who congratulates the piece and automatically to curse its detractors with a specific phrase — for an X, “your mother’s cunt” (mmá píma f’i) . Saramaka social structure: analysis of a maroon society in Surinam / By: Price, Richard, 1941- / Page 34)

Specify: participation in funeral:  “A master of ceremonies (sx w αs'a′lšəb) was hired by the deceased's family and issued a public invitation at the graveyard in an announcement following the burial; one form used was “so and so thanks you all, people, for coming to the funeral and he invites you all to come back to his house and eat.”” (9999) The structure of Twana culture Section: Observances after Burial By: Elmendorf, William W. (William Welcome), 1912- Page: 459Published: 9999Series: Monographic supplement (Washington State University. Research studies)

Specify: (Thanks to Pokohil the snakes are returned:  “Then these objects are returned to their owners and the snakes are emptied from their gourd container. The Indians form a circle about them on their knees, shaking chinchin . Then two Indians pick up the snakes and put them around the neck of the Woman, who holds them by heads and tails and dances thus. Then the First Indian takes the snakes and hangs them on the First Spaniard and dances with him. Then the Indian puts the snakes inside his own shirt and when the snakes wriggle out from sleeves or trousers, this part of the dance is ended. (After the dance the snakes are returned, with thanks, to Pokohil.) In the remainder of the dance the Indians and Spaniards fight over the Woman and each then dances with her, with suggestive movements.” Chichicastenango: the Kiche Indians; their history and culture; sacred symbols of their dress and textiles; Section: The Snake Dance. —; By: Rodas N., Flavio, 1881- Page: 84)

Specify: Performing an act of religious devotion “If a cousin or brother provides decisive backing, he may, as a sign of gratitude, perform an act of devotion, such as a period of daily prayer, or make a special contribution for the upkeep of the village mosque. In this case, God is thought to be a party to the vow and, by determining the course of events, makes possible the favour, even though it was performed by another person.” (1997) The Bajau Laut: adaptation, history, and fate in a maritime fishing society of south-east Sabah Section: Kinship Values By: Sather, Clifford Page: 241 Published: 1997 Series: South-East Asian social science monographs

Specify: Clapping  “Then Abini began to complain, saying, “Come on, I’ll say what we need and what was promised us (in the document appended to the treaty). Namely: 53 kegs of gunpowder, 13 long muskets, some light guns... After they listed all this, I asked if that was all, and they answered in unison, “Yes!”... Then they took the goods after having thanked the Honorable Court with handclapping. Such rhythmic handclapping, which is quiet and slow, is unlike Western applause. It is used in contexts of giving formal thanks, prayer, and asking a favor, as well as thanking me for my efforts, for they were certainly pleased about the division of the goods and again asked me to ask the Court if they might have the [additional] goods listed... Finally, all departed in good harmony after the division of the goods.”  Price, Richard. 1990. “Alabi’s World.” In Johns Hopkins Studies in Atlantic History and Culture, p. 49  Tying a cloth  “And the other one was going to take care of the washing. The mother said, “You’ll be giving me a proper burial indeed.” / íya/ She said to one of them, “Woman, you’ll really be burying me well.” / íya/ The last one said, “Every young man who comes here—” / íya/ (“yes” she said) “I’ll tie his belly [with a cloth, as a ritual protection and sign of gratitude].”  Price, Richard, and Sally Price. 1991. Two Evenings in Saramaka. Chicago: University of Chicago Press. p. 167
Specify: Other gestures related to interpersonal gratitude is smiting or striking the thigh; bowing or prostration; clapping of hands; and orans gestures.

This is a “day of sin” (dia pecado) , it is a sin to work on this day. The belief is that if one does not make his gifts to his parents during Holy Week he does so on this day. In the cofradía they give the drink to all who come, children as well as adults.” (1952) Chichicastenango: a Guatemalan village Section: Ascensión (May 5, 1932): By: Bunzel, Ruth Leah, 1898-1990 Page: 417Published: 1952Series: Publications of the American Ethnological Society

questions.name: Are gestures of interpersonal gratitude also seen as expressions of love, faithfulness, or devotion (as opposed to simply satisfying a feeling of obligation/indebtedness/need for balancing debts)?

answer_examples.answer: Yes [specify]: “The visitor honors the hut owner with his facial painting, and the host is appreciative of what the visitor has consciously striven to attain.” “If a visitor comes unexpectedly, however, the master of the hut does not reach for his painting material to decorate himself in the presence of his guest. He does this later on, returns the visit in the hut of the other, and in this way thanks him for the honor previously bestowed on him.” (1937) The Yahgan: the life and thought of the water nomads of Cape Horn Section: 3. Body Painting By: Gusinde, Martin, 1886-1969 Page: 96 “This painting is meant to express the fact that the visitor bestows on the other the pleasure of his coming and that he is happy to be there. That is why the master of the hut sooner or later responds likewise with a facial painting to express his pleasure over the visit and his gratitude toward the guest.” (1937) The Yahgan: the life and thought of the water nomads of Cape Horn Section: 3. Body Painting By: Gusinde, Martin, 1886-1969 Page: 97
Yes [specify]: Faithfulness and devotion were the main characteristics in terms of how this honor culture expressed gratitude: if someone did you well you showed "gratitude" by being loyal to them

Yes [specify]: Given out of magkalasa, meaning kindness and compassion, rather than being strictly transactional “The recipient of an act of magbuddi should acknowledge his gratitude by some form of return favour. However, the terms of repayment are never specified, and a return, while expected, cannot be demanded, but must be given, as was the original favour, out of magkalasa .” (1997) The Bajau Laut: adaptation, history, and fate in a maritime fishing society of south-east Sabah Section: Kinship Values By: Sather, Clifford Page: 240 Published: 1997 Series: South-East Asian social science monographs

Yes [specify]: In Ancient Near East texts, gestures of interpersonal gratitude are indeed seen not only as ways to satisfy obligation or balance debts but also as expressions of deeper emotions such as love, faithfulness, and devotion.

Yes [specify]: “In the presence of the whole assembly, the pretended discussion concerning the alms begins between the maternal uncle and the master of ceremonies. Assurance is given of the love of the family for the deceased, and of the care taken of him during his sickness. Finally permission is given for the cremation. Wine is poured, and the whole family kneels and thanks the maternal uncle. The master of ceremonies offers him, as keepsake and remembrance, a nice piece of woolen felt, some of the best clothes of the deceased, and some pieces of his jewelry. However, the maternal uncle must by custom refuse the gifts. The maternal uncle goes, followed by the whole assembly, to prostrate himself before the corpse. The dinner follows, in the open courtyard, after which the whole group prays Om Mani.” (The Monguors of the Kansu-Tibetan frontier: Part II. their religious life; Section: GUESTS AND THE MATERNAL UNCLE; Schram, Louis; Page: [p. 144(B))
Yes [specify]: Gestures of gratitude are also expressions of love, devotion, and faithfulness, not only repayment of debts.
Yes [specify]: Intergenerational sharing within families (see notes)

answer_examples.answer: Source 1 Description: This is a 19th century manuscript of Ppo Klaong Garai in the damnây (hymnal) genre from Palei Cang. The manuscript also includes Akhar Bani, which is a local variant of Arabic script.

Source 1 Description: This is a manuscript collection that was compiled over the course of the 18th through the 20th century and then photocopied. The images are of the photocopy. The manuscript includes Akayet Um Marup, Ariya Ppo Pareng, Dalikal Gru Churu, Dalikal Ppo Riyak, and Dalikal Ppo Klaong Garai. The original manuscript was given to Mr. Sam Van Tanh in 1975 and was originally his grandfather's. Thus, the photocopied form is of the final early 20th century form of the manuscript.

Source 2 Description: This manuscript is also a 19th century manuscript in the damnây (hymnal) genre, from Palei Pabhan. The manuscript also includes a section on the veneration of Ppo Ceng, one of the last kings of the Panduranga kingdom.

Source 3 Description: This manuscript has been handed down several generations, from the 18th century to the 20th century, although portions of the manuscript have clearly been added later or re-penned. The generations are as follows: Superior Priest Quang De (Thanh Y), Superior Priest Truong Van (Hieu Le), Gru urang Truong Huu (Phuoc Dong), Gru urang Truong Dat (Hieu Le). At present, the manuscript belongs to Basaih Quang So.

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: The Sanctuary became a major political site as well, which led to the establishment of a formal Treasury building by the Athenian delegation

Other [specify]: The most prized material offering in Cham rituals is the burning of agarwood (gahlau) incense. The cost of agarwood is quite notable. Procuring it has required relations with the Chamic-Austronesian upland communities (Jarai, Ede, Raglai, and Churu). In the case of Ppo Romé, this is particularly important, as one of his ritual names and historical reign names was Ppo Gihlau (the Sovereign of the Agarwood).

questions.name: Other
questions.parent_question: Is maintenance of the place performed:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: There were permanent priests at the sanctuary, who were augmented with regular visits from skilled maintenance and religious staff from various visiting delegations

Other [specify]: There are two clear forms of maintenance of this site. The first is official state maintenance performed by individuals who may or may not be ethnic Cham (but have, historically, been predominantly ethnic Vietnamese) who are hired by the provincial authority to oversee the site as a tourist destination. The other form of maintenance of this site is by the board of the Cham Ahiér priests of Ninh Thuận province. Each of the largest Cham Ahiér temples (Ppo Romé included) has a senior priest who sits on this board. In the most recent decade, the provincial authorities have begun to deem it more prudent to work with the priestly authority than in past decades. However, there is general discontent with the perception of neglect for Cham ritualistic requirements and practices dictating the forms of maintenance by provincial authorities.

questions.parent_question: Are formal burials present:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: The Ppo Romé temple-tower complex is thought to be the location of one of the oldest clan-based cenotaphs. We can think of these as cenotaphs because Cham Ahiér are traditionally cremated and their remains are usually "elsewhere." These are called "kut" in Cham. There is only one "kut" at the Ppo Romé tower. In other locations throughout the region, we might find numerous "kut" in a single location.

questions.name: Other
questions.parent_question: Does the supreme high god communicates with the living at this place:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: There is some question about the formality of what is a "religious specialist." There are female and, ever so occasionally, male, spirit mediums who might appear at religious ceremonies in addition to the formally recognized religious hierarchy. The Muk Pajau (female mediums) do appear to be more formally incorporated into the networks of the Ahiér priests and work collaboratively with them.

questions.name: Other
questions.parent_question: Do human spirits communicate with the living at this place:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: Ancestor spirits (muk kei) formally communicate with individuals who visit the place during prescribed rituals. Most often, ritual officiants have a more direct line of communication. However, members of the clans that are descended from Ppo Romé and his wives, are associated with communicating directly with muk kei at this site.

questions.name: Other
questions.parent_question: Do mixed human-divine beings communicate with the living at this place:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: Presuming that Ppo Romé spirit and the spirits of his wives, especially Bia Su Can and Bia Su Cih, are of mixed human and divine elements, being humans that were transformed into divinities. There is direct communication with them, although the preference is for them to communicate with the formal priest networks of the Cham Ahiér, the Muk Pajau, and then, members of the associated clan networks of Ppo Romé, the wives, and their descendants.

questions.name: Other
questions.parent_question: Is healing present/practiced at this place:

answer_examples.answer: Other [specify]: Healing at this place can also be psychological. There is a sense that "in the times of Champa" there was greater political autonomy for Cham communities. While individuals generally do not desire to return to those times (as they might have to experience "loss" again) there is a sense that there has been a form of psychological wound that has been inflicted. Communicating with the muk kei and divinities of the past times can help heal this wound, and allow individuals in the community to more effectively work for a better future.
